newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Mortar bomb hits family home in Bosnian town.
newsitem.headline: Mortar bomb hits family home in Bosnian town.

text.p: A Bosnian woman said her family narrowly missed injury when a mortar bomb crashed into her home in a weekend attack in the divided town of Mostar, a Sarajevo newspaper reported on Sunday.
The NATO-led peace force confirmed on Sunday that two 60mm mortar bombs were fired on Moslem-held eastern Mostar early on Saturday morning. One of the mortar bombs failed to explode.
A big explosion woke up Tidza Repesa at 1:05 a.m. on Saturday and showered her family with broken window glass, she told the daily newspaper Oslobodjenje.
Her husband and two children were also sleeping when the mortar bomb struck the wall of their home in the town centre near the Carinski bridge.
"We saw afterwards that it was a mortar (bomb) which hit the house wall near the window. If the mortar had fallen only 10 cm (inches) closer to the window, I am not sure we would be alive," she said.
It was the first report of a mortar attack in Mostar in peacetime, international officials said.
The peace agreement which halted the Bosnian war requires mortars, artillery and other heavy weapons to be stored at designated sites.
A spokesman for the multinational Stabilisation Force (SFOR) told Reuters there was no evidence to indicate the Bosnian Croat militia were involved in the mortar attack.
Major Andrew Saddleton said SFOR suspected "criminal elements" were responsible.
The firing of a mortar did not necessarily represent an "escalation" in tensions in Mostar and was probably an isolated incident, Saddleton said.
He said SFOR expects the former warring factions "to investigate what's going on down there and arrest those responsible".
Tensions have been running high in Mostar since armed Croat men opened fire last week on a group of Moslems trying to visit a cemetery in Croat-held western Mostar.
One man was killed and 22 wounded in the worst violence since the Dayton peace treaty was signed in December 1995.
According to witnesses and photographs possessed by NATO, Croat police in uniform stood by as men armed with guns and clubs assaulted the procession of 200 Moslems last Monday.
NATO has so far declined to release the photographs.
Two more explosions were reported on Saturday night in Mostar, which is strictly divided into Moslem and Croat sectors.
The source of the explosions, which caused no injuries or major damage, was unknown, Saddleton said.
International police monitors have reported hand grenades exploding nearly every night along the former front line over the past week. No injuries have been reporded.
